summary: Describes a framework for how users interact with SIP-based applications, focusing on stimulus signaling, in which a user agent sends inputs like key presses to guide an application.

eli5.summary: When you press keys during a phone menu, you are steering a program. This describes how that steering is sent in SIP.

questions: how do sip applications get user input
how does sip refer push a web page to a phone
subtitle: How SIP applications ask users for input, from key presses to web forms, without the phone knowing what the application does.

tldr.problem: Many SIP applications, such as prepaid calling cards, need input from the user, but phones cannot be taught the details of every application.
tldr.mechanism: The application hands the user agent a generic user interface component, described in a markup language. A REFER request pushes a web-style component, and a SUBSCRIBE request pushes a keypad filter whose results come back in NOTIFY requests. Alternatively the interface runs in the network and is reached through media streams.
tldr.outcome: The framework defines how user agents advertise support, how applications push, update and end interface components, and how a user agent authorizes them. Hard cases such as input on a phone with only a keypad are left open.

today: RFC 5629 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the framework that describes stimulus interaction for SIP applications.

sections.title: Why Applications Need User Input
sections.content:
A SIP application is a program running on a SIP element, such as a proxy or user agent, that adds value for a user or administrator. The RFC lists prepaid calling card calls, conferencing and presence-based call routing as examples.

Most applications need input to work. A prepaid calling card application needs the card number, a PIN and the destination number. The process of giving input to an application is called application interaction.

Interaction is either functional, where the user device understands the application's semantics, or stimulus, where it does not. Stimulus interaction lets new applications be built without changing the user device, and it is the subject of this framework.
sections.eli5: Some programs need you to type or say something, like a secret code. This document is about how the program asks, even when your phone has never heard of that program.

sections.title: The Interaction Model
sections.content:
The model has a chain: the user gives input to a user device, the device passes it to a user interface, and the interface turns it into an event for the application. The application may update the interface in return. The RFC calls the separation between user interface and application absolutely fundamental to the framework.

It then sorts systems along four axes.

  • Functional or stimulus: a functional interface knows the application and is usually faster and friendlier, but needs standardized protocols. A stimulus interface is generic and slower, but allows new applications without standardization. The web is the RFC's example of a stimulus interface.
  • Real-time or non-real-time: non-real-time interaction happens by provisioning, for example setting a call-forward number on a web page.
  • Client-local or client-remote: the interface either runs with the user device or in the network, reached through media such as audio or video.
  • Presentation-capable or presentation-free: a presentation-capable interface can show feedback after each input, like a web page. A presentation-free one only collects input and cannot easily support a focus, the choice of which interface gets the input.
sections.eli5: Think of a vending machine. You press buttons (the device), the panel decides what you meant (the interface), and the machine inside does the work (the application). Keeping the panel separate from the machine is the big idea.

sections.title: Telephone Scenarios and Deployment Topologies
sections.content:
The RFC takes a telephone to be a device with a 12-key keypad, a speaker and a microphone. On the PSTN the interface is almost always client-remote, with keypad input sent as DTMF. In SIP the media travels over RTP, and keypad input can be sent as DTMF tones or, preferably, encoded as described in RFC 4733.

A client-local alternative puts the whole interface on the phone, for example a VoiceXML browser, or a Keypad Markup Language (KPML) request document for phones without a display. A third pattern, flip-flop, installs a small local component that waits for a trigger such as a long pound key press, and only then connects the user to a remote interface that plays announcements. The benefit is cost, since no media stream is needed while waiting for the trigger.

Four topologies are described.

  • Third-party application: outside the dialog, learning of it out of band, for example through the dialog event package.
  • Co-resident application: inside one of the user agents, common in protocol converters and gateways.
  • Third-party application with a user device proxy: the component sits in an intermediary that relays media.
  • Proxy application: inside a transaction stateful, record-routing proxy, common in routing applications.
sections.eli5: The menu can live inside your phone, or out in the network where your voice travels to it. Sometimes a tiny helper in your phone just waits for a special button, and then the big menu gets switched on.

sections.title: Pushing Interface Components
sections.content:
A user interface component is a piece of interface that runs independently of others. It is always tied to a dialog: it can be created once the dialog or early dialog exists, and it ends when the dialog ends.

For a client-local, presentation-capable component, the application sends a REFER to the user agent's GRUU. The Refer-To header holds an HTTP URI pointing at the markup, and a Target-Dialog header names the dialog. Later input goes back by HTTP form POST, and the reply is the next page of markup.

For a presentation-free component, the application sends a SUBSCRIBE using the KPML event package. Its body is the markup that says when to report input, and reports come back as NOTIFY requests. Such a component works in one of two modes: one shot, which reports once, or monitor, which stays until the dialog ends.

An application MUST NOT push a component until it has confirmed the user agent's capabilities and the dialog exists. It SHOULD put its name in the From display name.

Updating and ending differ by type. A presentation-free filter is updated with a SUBSCRIBE refresh and ended with Expires of zero. A presentation-capable component cannot be updated asynchronously or ended by the application, so the application must be ready to time out waiting for input.
sections.eli5: The program sends your phone a note saying 'show this page' or 'tell me when the user presses these keys.' The page version lets you click around, and the keypad version just reports your button presses.

sections.title: What a User Agent Must Do
sections.content:
To take part, a user agent advertises its abilities in dialog-initiating requests and responses.

  • For presentation-capable components it MUST support REFER and list it in Allow, support the target dialog specification and include the tdialog option tag in Supported, support user agent capabilities, and put a schemes parameter naming HTTP in its Contact. It MUST list the markups it accepts in Accept, and the RFC recommends HTML support.
  • For presentation-free components it MUST support SUBSCRIBE and the KPML event package, and at minimum the application/kpml-request+xml type.
  • For both kinds it MUST support GRUU and carry a GRUU in Contact, with gruu and tdialog in Supported.

These headers should not be encrypted, because proxies running applications read them. A third-party application off the call path can learn capabilities another way, such as the registration event package.

When input is mapped to components, a PC window manager picks the component with focus. On a device where the user cannot choose, input is assumed to belong to all client-local components, and for client-remote ones it is sent as media, typically using RFC 4733.
sections.eli5: Before a phone can play along, it has to announce 'I can do web pages' or 'I can report key presses.' It is like a sign on a shop door that lists what the shop accepts.

sections.title: Authorization and Security
sections.content:
Because a network application can place a user interface on a client, the main requirement is authorization: knowing the provider is allowed to do this matters more than knowing its name. A user agent SHOULD try to authenticate the sender, but digest authentication is unlikely to help because the user agent rarely shares a secret with an application. Identity mechanisms such as RFC 4474 can help.

The user agent MAY have pre-set policies. Otherwise the RFC recommends automatic authorization if the application proves it is on the call path, or trusted by an element on it, by presenting the dialog identifiers in Target-Dialog or the KPML Event parameters. This is only safe if the user agent uses cryptographically random identifiers, with at least 128 bits of randomness, and SIPS for its dialogs. Without both, the application MUST NOT be automatically authorized.

A request with no valid dialog identifier MUST be rejected with a 403. If user approval is needed, the user agent SHOULD answer with a 202, and for a REFER it MUST NOT act on the URI until approval is given.
sections.eli5: Before letting a program put a menu on your phone, the phone checks that it really knows about your call. The secret call numbers are long and random so nobody can guess them.

sections.title: Feature Interaction Between Interfaces
sections.content:
Feature interaction is the problem that arises when several applications or components want to serve one user at once. For stimulus signaling it comes down to deciding which interface an input is meant for.

With client-local interfaces it is easier, because the device knows each application and can use focus determination. A PC window manager does this, and a phone with a button beside each display can allocate buttons per application. A phone with only a 12-key keypad is a focusless device. The RFC makes no normative recommendation but concludes the best option is to send the input to all interfaces unless the markup asks to suppress it, as the PSTN does. Key events are then sent in all audio streams as RFC 4733 events. Providing a better mechanism than the PSTN on such devices is an explicit non-goal.

For client-remote interfaces, focus is much harder and left out of scope. Conflicts inside one application are milder, since the application can avoid overlapping inputs, and tight coupling between components, as in multimodal interfaces, is best handled by markups that support it.
sections.eli5: If two programs are both listening and you press a button, who is it for? A computer lets you click a window to choose. A simple phone cannot, so the button press goes to everyone listening.

sections.title: Example Call Flow
sections.content:
The worked example is a call-recording application that lets the caller start recording by clicking a button in a web form. The application sits on the call path as the domain's proxy.

Caller A calls B through the application (messages 1 to 6). The caller's INVITE advertises GRUU, Target-Dialog, REFER and the schemes parameter. The application then sends a REFER to A's GRUU carrying a Target-Dialog (message 7). A answers 200 OK, reports progress with a NOTIFY, and, because the REFER carried a valid dialog identifier over TLS with sufficiently random identifiers, authorizes the application automatically. A fetches the page with an HTTP GET (message 11), and when the user clicks the link the result is POSTed to the server and a new display returns (messages 15 and 16).
sections.eli5: You are on a call and a record button pops up on your screen. Your phone checked that the button really came from the call's helper, loaded the page, and told the helper when you clicked.

messages.label: INVITE
messages.note: Caller advertises GRUU, Target-Dialog and REFER support.

messages.label: REFER
messages.note: Refer-To is an HTTP URI; Target-Dialog names the call.

messages.label: HTTP GET
messages.note: A authorizes the application and fetches the web page.

messages.label: HTTP POST
messages.note: The user's click is sent back; a new display returns.
